content.p: Logan Mwangi was five years old when his body was found in the River Ogmore, in the Welsh village of Sarn near Bridgend, on the morning of 31 July 2021. He was lying partly in the water, in dinosaur pyjama bottoms and a Spider-Man top, about 250 metres from his home. His mother had reported him missing from that home that morning. Within days, police had arrested her, her partner and the partner's stepson, and a trial at Cardiff Crown Court later ended with all three being convicted of his murder, though the judge said it was not possible to be sure exactly what had happened to him at home.

On 21 April 2022 a jury found his mother, Angharad Williamson, his stepfather, John Cole, and a 13-year-old boy who had just moved into the household guilty of murder. They were sentenced on 30 June 2022 to life terms with minimum periods of 28 years, 29 years and 15 years. The case then became a test of Welsh child protection, because Logan had been seen by doctors, social workers and police in the year before he died.
content.h2: A child known to his school
content.p: Logan was born in Bridgend on 15 March 2016. His father, Benjamin Mwangi, is a bookmaker of Kenyan heritage who lived in Essex; the relationship with Williamson ended within months of the birth, and the Guardian reported that she moved back to Wales. Logan's teachers at Tondu Primary School described a bright, polite boy who loved the outdoor classroom and who, in the school's words, was always smiling. His favourite character was Spider-Man. He had a slight stammer.

Williamson, then 30, was raised in Essex and had a record of two theft charges from 2014, according to Wales Online. In 2017 she married a soldier; the marriage ended after he was convicted of attacking her. In spring 2019 she met John Cole, a man from Rugby in Warwickshire, in a Bridgend pub. Cole had moved to Wales in 2017. His past included convictions for assault, battery and perverting the course of justice, and the BBC reported that three of his earlier convictions were for perverting the course of justice. Former friends told reporters he had been linked to the National Front and was "very racist", and he had told people he served in the SAS, which the Guardian described as false.

After Cole entered Logan's life, people close to the family said the boy's world shrank. His grandmother, Clare Williamson, told the court that Cole came between her and her daughter, and the sleepovers at her home stopped. Friends said Cole told them he did not like Logan, and the Guardian reported that he nicknamed the boy "Coco Pop" because of his skin colour and resented how closely Logan resembled his father. Prosecutors told the jury that Cole's attitude towards Logan, a child of mixed race, was relevant to the way he was dehumanised.

On 16 August 2020 Logan was taken to hospital with a broken arm after, his mother said, a fall down the stairs. Staff alerted the authorities because of a delay in bringing him in. During the hospital visit a paediatric doctor took 31 images of other injuries, including bruises to his forehead, ears, cheeks and arm. The consultant judged the injuries accidental and made no child protection referral. Months later, in early 2021, Williamson told police that Craig Mulligan, then living locally, had confessed to pushing Logan down the stairs.

Logan's family was on the child protection register in Wales. By March 2021, because of worries about Cole, Logan and his younger sibling had their own social worker. In June 2021, a month before his death, the family was taken off the register, which meant the agencies no longer believed he faced a risk of significant harm. In the weeks before he died he also had a broken collarbone that was never treated. The Guardian reported that the couple told social services that a burn on the back of his neck came from a hot tap, although Cole later claimed in evidence that Williamson had burned him with a hot coffee spoon.

The boy who would be tried alongside them had a different history. Mulligan was not related to Logan, Cole or Williamson, but Cole had raised him from the age of nine months. About six months before the killing he was taken into local authority care after his mother assaulted him. A foster family said he repeatedly told them he wanted to kill Logan, whom he called "the five-year-old". They said they passed the threats to his social worker, who denied in the witness box that she had been told. On 26 July 2021 a family court gave Cole parental responsibility for Mulligan, without knowing of the threats, according to the Guardian, and the teenager moved into the Sarn flat. Prosecutors compared the decision to throwing a lit match into a powder keg.

Logan tested positive for Covid-19 on 20 July, according to the BBC (the Guardian gives 21 July). He was kept in his bedroom behind a baby gate, a room Williamson accepted in court was like a "dungeon". When food was brought, he had to face the wall. The judge later said this was "extreme" and the culmination of treatment that had dehumanised him in the eyes of his parents. His stammer worsened, he wet himself more often and he began to harm himself by pinching and biting. On 29 July Mulligan's social worker made an unscheduled visit and was not let in, on the pretext that Logan was isolating, according to Wales Online.

What happened inside the flat on 29 and 30 July was never fully established. The judge said that because he was killed at home "it is not possible to be sure what has happened to him". Williamson's account, given after several police interviews, was that on Thursday 29 July Cole punched Logan twice in the stomach after an argument over a damaged stereo and that Mulligan then swept him to the floor with a martial arts move. Cole admitted shaking Logan by the arms but denied hitting him that day. The pathologist, Dr John Williams, found 56 external injuries and told the jury that damage to the liver, bowel and duodenum resembled what is seen after a fall from a great height or a high-speed road crash. His evidence was that Logan may have survived for several hours after the injuries were inflicted.
content.h2: The river and the false alarm
content.p: CCTV from nearby houses showed Cole and Mulligan leaving the flat at 2.43am on 31 July with Logan's body in a sports bag, according to the BBC. They crossed to the river and left him there. They went home, then went out again to dispose of the dinosaur pyjama top he had been wearing; police later found it in woodland with a large cut in it. At about 5.46am Williamson rang 999 in what ITV described as a 13-minute call, saying that she had tucked her son in and that he was gone. Prosecutors called this a "callous" and "elaborate" cover-up. Her phone showed she had been awake during the night, and cameras recorded the light in Logan's room being switched on and off.

Police found Logan in the river in Pandy Park. All three were arrested on 4 August. Williamson told the arresting officers she had done nothing wrong. In his interview, Mulligan said he had helped Cole throw away garden rubbish and had not known whether Logan was in the bags; he claimed Williamson was lying to get out of the cells.

The trial opened in February 2022. Williamson and Mulligan pleaded not guilty to murder and to perverting the course of justice; Cole denied murder but pleaded guilty to the cover-up charge. The two adults also faced a charge of causing or allowing a child's death, which both denied. Williamson told the jury she had slept through the night. The defendants blamed one another, and the court heard Williamson call out to Cole to "tell the truth". The jury returned guilty verdicts on 21 April. Williamson collapsed screaming "no" as they were read.

Sentencing was on 30 June. Mrs Justice Jefford said the attack was "nothing short of horrifying" and told the three they were "all responsible for Logan's death". She said she was sure Cole and Mulligan had carried out the assault, but did not believe Williamson took part in it physically. She rejected Williamson's version that she had run from the house for help after the earlier attack, calling it "made up after the event to protect yourself and shift the blame", and said that Logan was "for the most part of Friday injured or dying" while his mother did nothing. She described the cover-up as "careful and calculated and not the product of panic". Cole received a minimum of 29 years, Williamson 28 and Mulligan 15.

Mulligan's identity was protected during the trial because of his age. The judge lifted the order at sentencing, saying naming him would help the public understand the family dynamics and let a safeguarding inquiry be properly reported. She told him she was sure he had acted as Cole told him to, or to copy him: "You idolised him and wanted to gain his approval." Logan's father said in a statement that his son was the "sweetest and most beautiful boy" and that he was devastated he could not protect him.

The Cwm Taf Morgannwg Safeguarding Board's Child Practice Review, published on 23 November 2022, covered the 17 months before Logan's death and referred to him as Child T. Its independent chair, Jan Pickles, called the failure to share the August 2020 injuries a "significant missed opportunity". Had the information reached social services it "most likely", though she said this could not be known for sure given hindsight, would have triggered a child protection assessment. The review said health staff were reluctant to challenge more senior clinicians, and that some who were uncomfortable about the hospital assessment did not use whistleblowing procedures.

It found that Logan's voice "was not heard" and that the complicated adult relationships around him obscured professionals' view of the child. Covid-19 had cut one-to-one sessions away from home and the family had used the pandemic as a barrier to engagement. Risk plans had been stepped down without clear reasons, and an adult the review calls Adult A, who it said seemed able to manipulate his partners and some professionals, had not been examined closely enough. Children's services did not tell Logan's father of their involvement. The review also recorded that a social worker called on Mulligan the day before Logan died, with no legal power to go inside. It made 10 local recommendations and five for Wales as a whole, including that family courts consider a 12-week minimum for social worker assessments where this case allowed only four. The review praised the police response and Logan's school.

Wales's deputy minister for social services, Julie Morgan, apologised to Logan's father. The Welsh Government had earlier declined to hold an independent review of children's social work, which the BBC reported was backed by the Conservatives, Plaid Cymru and the Liberal Democrats, and which Cardiff University's Prof Donald Forrester also supported.

A juror told the Mirror, as reported by The Week, that the trial left her with recurring nightmares. The judge excused the jury from future service. Campaigners questioned whether the family court papers about Mulligan should be published, and the National Association for Youth Justice used the case to argue for rethinking how children who kill are sentenced.

In 2025 an inquest heard that Logan's grandmother, Clare Williamson, 64, died after falling from a cliff near Bridgend in a suspected suicide, LBC reported. In January 2023 the Court of Appeal had refused Williamson's bid to overturn her conviction. In July 2026 a pre-inquest review into Logan's death was held at the South Wales Central Coroner's Court in Pontypridd. Williamson, who appeared by video link from prison, was represented by former police officer Tony Thompson, who said he was looking at whether she could apply to the Criminal Cases Review Commission and that she maintains her innocence. A full inquest was expected later in 2026.
